title: Wise attention
hook: don't ask "did I exist in the past"; ask "what is dukkha, what ends it" (MN 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: asava, and your line, seven ways. Which way did you choose, and did you get to use it once? Day four hundred four.

Three in the morning, and the questions start. Who am I, really? What was I before all this? Will any of it matter? What if I've got everything wrong? You can turn those over for hours and get up more tired than you lay down. About twenty-five centuries ago, the Buddha listed nearly the same questions, almost one for one. And then he said something surprising about them. Today: wise attention.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `WHO AM I? WHAT WAS I?` → `TIRED BY SUNRISE.`

segments.voice: In MN 2, the first of the seven ways with the taints is seeing, and seeing depends on how you attend. The Buddha describes unwise attention first. A person wonders: Was I in the past? Was I not? What was I in the past? How was I? Will I be in the future? What will I be? And about now: Am I? Am I not? What am I? Where did this being come from, and where will it go? Then they settle on a view. I have a self. Or, I have no self. Or some other. And the Buddha calls all of these a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a fetter of views. Notice that even I have no self is on that list, as a view to get tangled in. Then wise attention. The Pali is yoniso manasikara. Manasikara is attention, literally making in the mind. Yoniso comes from yoni, a womb, a source: attention that goes back to where things come from. And here is what it attends to: this is dukkha; this is its arising; this is its ending; this is the way to its ending. The four noble truths, used as questions. He doesn't call the big questions forbidden or foolish. He says they loop. The useful question is one that changes something: where is the suffering in this, what's feeding it, what would ease it? And the text says attention like this cuts three fetters: the view of a fixed self, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals. Not a small result, for changing what you ask.
screen: `WAS I? AM I? WHAT AM I?` · `A THICKET OF VIEWS.` · `YONISO — BACK TO THE SOURCE.` · `WHAT IS DUKKHA? WHAT ENDS IT?` · then, large: `THE USEFUL QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sit, and find a question that's been circling lately. Why does this always happen to me? What's wrong with me? Hold it for a breath. Then try turning it into a question about right now. Where is the tension in this, in the body? What's feeding it? What would ease it, even a little? You don't need answers. Just notice how the new question feels different in the chest. The bell holds the time.
Wise attention. Yoniso manasikara: attention that goes back to the source, and asks what is suffering and what ends it.
Your line: the useful question. Today, when a looping question starts, swap it once for this: what would ease this, right now? Day four hundred four.

howItsDone: Teachers in many Buddhist schools emphasize wise attention, yoniso manasikara, as the ground of practice; Theravada teachers often present the four noble truths as a way of looking at any experience.

match.prompt: match the words of wise attention.
pairs: what is dukkha, what ends it

myth: the Buddha calls the big questions about the self foolish
he says they lead into a thicket of views, not out of dukkha.
in MN 2, even 'I have no self' is listed among the views
it's one of the views unwise attention settles on.
wise attention cuts three fetters, the text says
the view of a fixed self, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals.

fork.setup: it's 3 a.m. and you're asking: what was I in the past? what does MN 2 suggest?
options: keep thinking until you find the answer
ask instead: what is dukkha here, and what ends it?
decide you have no self and go back to sleep
fork.reveal: MN 2 turns attention to the four truths: this is dukkha, its arising, its ending, the way. even 'I have no self' is listed as a view to get stuck in.

original.note: Pali yoniso manasikāra: wise attention, attention by way of the source.

trapdoor: what you thought: wise attention means paying close attention.
what it means: attention that goes back to the source and asks what suffering is and what ends it.
what a scholar hears: yoniso is an adverb from yoni, womb or origin; MN 2 lists six views, including both 'I have a self' and 'I have no self', as products of unwise attention.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta (taints abandoned by seeing)

notes: The list of questions from MN 2 is paraphrased and shortened.
MN 2's six views ('I have a self', 'I have no self', etc.) and the three fetters cut: please confirm.
'Twenty-five centuries' is approximate; the Buddha's dates are debated.
